article.title: Viewing and fixing security alerts in the GitHub Copilot app - GitHub Docs
article.text:
Viewing and fixing security alerts in the GitHub Copilot app
Work through code scanning alerts alongside your code using the GitHub security extension for the GitHub Copilot app.
Who can use this feature?
The GitHub Copilot app is available for all Copilot plans.
Download the GitHub Copilot app
In this article
Note
The GitHub security extension is in public preview and subject to change.
About the GitHub security extension
The GitHub security extension lets you find, understand, and fix code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. You can also review your local changes for new vulnerabilities before opening a pull request.
You install the extension as part of the github-security plugin. The extension provides a canvas labeled Security, where you can work with existing alerts and run local security reviews alongside your session.
Prerequisites
To use the GitHub security extension, you need:
A Copilot plan and the GitHub Copilot app, signed in to your GitHub account. See Getting started with the GitHub Copilot app.
Permission to install the github-security plugin under your enterprise's managed settings, if configured.
If you use Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise, the GitHub Copilot app policy must be enabled. If access to the app or plugin is blocked, contact your administrator.
To view existing code scanning alerts for a repository in the Security canvas, you also need access to the alerts for the repository, with code scanning enabled. Private repositories require GitHub Code Security. See Configuring default setup for code scanning.
The extension supports repositories on GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. GitHub Enterprise Server is not supported.
You do not need code scanning enabled or a GitHub Code Security license to run a local security review.
Installing the GitHub security extension
To install the plugin from the terminal using Copilot CLI, enter:
Shell
copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot
copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot
Alternatively, install the plugin in the GitHub Copilot app:
In the app sidebar, click Customize.
In the search bar, search for github-security.
Under Plugins, next to "github-security," click + Install.
After installation, the plugin and its extension are automatically enabled.
Viewing code scanning alerts in the Security canvas
Use the extension to view open code scanning alerts in your repository, ordered by severity. Code scanning must be enabled for the repository, and you must have access to its alerts.
Start a new session for the repository you want to work on.
If the Security canvas isn't already open, click , hover over Canvas, then click Security.
On the extension's Security canvas home page, click Code scanning findings.
To narrow the list, in the upper-right corner of the canvas, click to show the search and filter controls.
Click an alert's title to view its description, severity, and affected code in the canvas.
Check the alert's linked pull requests to see whether someone is already working on a fix. To open the full alert page on GitHub, hover over the alert's row, click , then click Open in browser.
The extension shows code scanning alerts, not Dependabot or secret scanning alerts.
Understanding and fixing alerts
The Explain and Fix buttons ask the Copilot agent in your session to act on the selected code scanning alerts:
Explain asks the agent to explain the alerts so you can understand the vulnerabilities before deciding how to address them.
Fix asks the agent to change your code to address the alerts.
To work on a single alert, click on it to open its details or hover over it in the findings list to reveal the Explain and Fix buttons. To work on multiple alerts, select the checkboxes next to them.
Click the Explain or Fix button.
Review the agent's response in the session. If you requested a fix, review the diff and run the relevant tests for your project.

article.title: Your Agent Will Pick the Hackable One
article.text:
← geoffstearns.com
Your Agent Will Pick the Hackable One
Geoff Stearns · November 15, 2026
The M-VAVE FM-1 is a pocket FM synthesizer that sells for about $70, and almost nobody who owns one still runs the firmware it shipped with. Owners started writing their own in September. By October there were too many to cover in one article: a virtual analog synth, a multitrack groovebox, a dark ambient sampler, and a port of Doom. Yes, the video game. Going by what the developers post on the forums, nearly all of them were written with AI coding tools.
Video: Custom Firmware Tierlist by AudioPilz, ranking FM-1 firmwares.
Then M-Vave did something uncommon for a hardware company. In October it published its own firmware as open source under GPLv3, along with a development kit and a browser emulator for testing custom builds before you flash them.
I think this is where most consumer gadgets that run their own firmware are headed: synths, TVs, routers, printers. When software is cheap to write, the firmware a device ships with is just the first version. Devices that let owners replace it will sell better than devices that don’t. Most buyers won’t care about that. Their AI agents will, and more buying decisions are going to run through agents.
Owners already replace the software
When a device doesn’t do what its owner wants, most people put up with it. Some replace the software, and in a few categories that’s already normal.
Cheap retro handhelds from Anbernic and others ship with firmware that buyers usually replace within days, and muOS and Knulli are the standard recommendations. Pebble came back as a fully open project. Core Devices published the OS, the phone apps, and the hardware schematics, and the phone app can install from app stores anyone can run. I replaced the home screen on our Google TV, which runs Android, with a custom launcher built for our family, with no ads and no tracking. Ubiquiti owners hook their network controllers up to AI agents through community-built servers and have the agent audit firewall rules and tune the network. That isn’t new firmware, but the agent is already running the device.
Writing firmware got cheap
Writing firmware used to mean reverse engineering the chip, learning a vendor’s toolchain, and weeks of trial and error. The FM-1 runs on a JieLi chip with little public documentation, and owners still had working firmware within weeks.
AI made each part of that cheaper. It can read undocumented code, write new code for an unfamiliar chip, and build the editors, installers, and emulators around it. A motivated owner can now get through all of it in a weekend. Once that’s true, any device with writable flash is a platform, whether the maker planned for it or not.
Agents will do the installing
Most people don’t think about improving their devices. They use what they get. So right now custom firmware reaches a small group: a few people write it, and a somewhat larger group finds it and installs it.
I don’t expect that to last. As agents take on more everyday work, the owner stops being the one who installs things. You ask your agent to fix something that bugs you about a device. It tries a setting first. If that doesn’t work, it looks for firmware someone else wrote, forks the closest match, or writes its own. You see that the problem went away, and you may never know the device is running custom code.
How fast this happens depends more on the hardware than on AI. The device has to accept new firmware, and signed firmware and locked bootloaders stop that. The agent needs a way in, like USB or a browser tool such as M-Vave’s Workbench. And a bad install has to be recoverable, since an agent can’t open the case and fix a bricked board. M-Vave added a tool that puts the stock firmware back in about ten seconds.
Your agent will pick the hackable one
This changes how people buy hardware. Ask your agent which TV, router, or synth to get, and it will lean toward the one it can change, because that’s the one…

article.title: The Claude Delusion
article.text:
Signs of Triviality
Opinions, mostly my own, on the importance of being and other things.
[homepage]
[blog]
[jschauma@netmeister.org]
[@jschauma]
[RSS]
The Claude Delusion
November 13th, 2026
Something weird happens to people who are successful.
They start to think they're gods.
Actually accomplishing anything is obviously no strict
pre-requisite of success. And maybe it's not so much
"being successful", but rather "being rich". How do
you become rich? Some people are just lucky. Lucky
to have a physical talent, lucky to have parents able
and willing to nurture your talent, and of course
quite often lucky to have been at
the right place at the right time1.
Being lucky doesn't mean they didn't also
work hard. But even—especially!—the Paris
Hiltons of the world, the children of Hollywood
superstars, the crooks starting their corrupt empires
with "a
small loan" (or a share of an emerald mine) from
their fathers—they all
strongly believe that they deserve their
success and then conclude that anybody not as
successful only has themselves to blame.
This is especially the case for people in tech, where
for years and years being good at programming has been
equated with overall (and often: superior)
intelligence2, and those
illusory superiority effects then amplify rampant
Dunning-Kruger to quickly turn "I am good at
writing code, and with some luck, I managed to be
successful" into a train of thought that goes
more like "I am successful. Success is not random,
so I must deserve my success. I appear to be a
genius, I've mastered coding, anything else is
trivial. Ergo, I am good at everything."
Bill Gates, MD / PhD Biology
Let's take Bill Gates as an example.
Now, mind you,
Bill Gates certainly has accomplished a lot, and his
skillset and professional background includes without
a doubt a lot of computer programming and various
ruthless monopolistic business tactics. In a
recent New York Times interview, he describes how
he evaluated OpenAI's level of progress
(emphasis mine):
And I was going down to see OpenAI on a regular basis
to see the work they were doing, and I challenged
them, saying: Hey, if you can read a biology textbook
and pass the advanced placement exam — getting a
perfect grade, which is a 5 — then you will have
proven that you are reading. That is, encoding
knowledge in an accessible form.
And so it’s six months before the public release that
Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever come to
my house and demonstrate to me getting a 5 on the A.P.
exam, even on questions that I had made up that it
couldn't possibly have seen — very complex biology
problems. It was nearly perfect. So that was shock No.1.
Now Bill Gates surely has shown an interest in biology
and, through his work with the Bill & Melinda
Gates Foundation, has probably read a lot of articles
and research in this field. But the hubris to think
himself a subject matter expert able to make up advanced,
novel questions in a scientific field outside
his own and suitable to assess AI's true capabilities
and then being "shocked" that it could
answer these questions makes my point.
Although, what really cooks his noodle is the idea that AI
can do what he used to do: write code.
And then late last year, when Anthropic's Claude
coding models got super good, I could see that they
are as good as I am — it’s significantly my most
developed talent, because I was obsessed from age 13
to 24 as to whether I could write code as good or
better than anyone.
That’s another moment where I went: This is
incredible. That the capability of doing long-running,
complex tasks has now gotten to the point that they
are superhuman at writing code and in finding flaws in
code.
Take note of the emphasis I added: the very notion
that something else could be "as good as I
am" is, first of all, hard to believe and
secondly necessarily means that it's
"superhuman". That man is not lacking
self-esteem, no sirree, Bob.
Likewise, this is also where many of the tech bros
appear to be losing…

article.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source
article.text:
All AI-generated code should be Open Source
Jakub T. Jankiewicz
This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.
First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.
The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.
However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.
Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.
If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.
